(CNN) -- Robert Barnett, a prominent Washington attorney, has worked on eight national presidential campaigns, focusing on debate preparation. He played the role of George H.W. Barnett: The individuals will not necessarily express the question as a journalist would. So, for example, one of these people will probably not ask about Internal Revenue Service Code section 341, but rather will ask about their taxes and their tax burdens and what they care about with respect to taxation. And so you have to be very careful to be sure you understand what the individual is asking about and you have to be particularly careful to answer the question, because if you don't, you risk alienating the questioner and the audience and the listeners. CNN: You're in a unique position. You have prepped, I think, seven or eight presidential campaigns. You've done debate prep, you've stood in and played the role of Dick Cheney and others. What's that like? What are you trying to do to prepare the candidate, any candidate? Barnett:  If I'm playing the surrogate, if you will, if I'm the Republican for a Democrat, I try to prepare myself -- not to imitate; I'm not Darrell Hammond or Dana Carvey. I'm not that talented. But I try to be ready with what my candidate that I'm playing, if you will, has said -- the exact words used, the way they counterattack, the way they attack. And I try to make sure that the candidate I'm working with, meaning the Democrat, has heard just about everything that they could hear from their opponent before they ever walk on the stage. CNN: Do you try to bait them, get them to bite a little and then say that's not what you should be doing? Barnett: Well, it can get pretty contested. When I prepared with Rep. Geraldine Ferraro in 1984 when she was running against then-vice president George Herbert Walker Bush, I baited her a lot and she got so angry with me that she frequently walked over to me and slugged me on the arm. So I left the process black and blue. CNN: When you're doing that sort of thing, how direct can you be with the candidate? Or do you have to treat them with a bit of kid gloves? Barnett: I treat them with no kid gloves. It's fair to say I'm direct, I make sure they hear everything from me before they hear it on the stage and maybe hear it even a little more aggressively so they can be prepared.

# Robert Barnett: Behind-the-Scenes Debate Coach

(CNN) -- For decades, Robert Barnett, a well-known attorney based in Washington, has lent his expertise to eight national presidential campaigns, specializing specifically in preparing candidates for debates. During mock debate sessions, he took on the persona of George H.W. Bush when helping Geraldine Ferraro prepare in 1984, and again when working with Michael Dukakis in 1988. Throughout the 1992 election cycle, he sparred with Bill Clinton in more than 20 practice sessions. His portfolio also includes standing in as Dick Cheney during both the 2000 and 2004 elections, as well as guiding Hillary Clinton through preparation for all 23 primary debates in her bid for the 2008 nomination. In an interview with CNNI's Michael Holmes, Barnett—who has faced off against Democratic candidates ranging from Ferraro to Clinton in these rehearsal sessions—shared insights into his unique role.

**CNN: What sets Tuesday's town hall debate apart from typical debate formats?**

**Barnett:** Unlike trained journalists, everyday citizens won't phrase their questions using technical language. Nobody attending will likely bring up something like Internal Revenue Service Code section 341—instead, they'll speak plainly about their own taxes and what concerns them personally about the tax system. This means candidates must listen carefully to grasp the real intent behind each question, and they need to actually address what's being asked. Dodging a question here carries real risk—it can turn off both the person asking and everyone else watching or listening.

**CNN: You occupy a distinctive niche in this world. Having prepared candidates for what sounds like seven or eight presidential races, you've literally embodied figures like Dick Cheney during practice sessions. Walk us through that experience—what's the goal when prepping any candidate?**

**Barnett:** When I'm playing the opposing role—say, standing in as the Republican candidate for a Democrat I'm helping—my goal isn't to do an impression. I'm no Darrell Hammond or Dana Carvey; I don't have that kind of performative skill. Instead, I focus on mastering the substance: what my "character" has actually said, their specific phrasing, how they go on offense or defense. My aim is to make sure the candidate I'm coaching has essentially heard every possible line of attack from their rival before ever stepping onto the actual stage.

**CNN: Do you deliberately provoke them—try to get a rise out of them just to point out afterward that reacting that way would be a mistake?**

**Barnett:** Things can definitely heat up. Back in 1984, when I helped Geraldine Ferraro prepare to face then-Vice President George H.W. Bush, I pushed her buttons repeatedly. She got so frustrated with me that she'd actually walk over and punch my arm. I came out of that whole process covered in bruises.

**CNN: During these sessions, how blunt are you allowed to be? Or do you have to soften your approach somewhat?**

**Barnett:** There's no softening it—I'm about as direct as it gets. My philosophy is that they should hear the toughest version of an attack from me first, sometimes even more forcefully than they'll encounter on the actual stage, so they walk in fully ready for anything.

Unlike conventional debates, where trained journalists pose pointed, often adversarial questions, town hall debates feature questions from ordinary citizens. This shift changes the entire dynamic of the exchange. Candidates must not only listen carefully but also interpret the underlying intent behind a citizen's question—whether it concerns taxes, healthcare, or another personal issue—and respond in a way that feels direct, genuine, and relevant to that individual's concern.

# The Debate Whisperer: Inside Robert Barnett's Decades of Prepping Presidential Candidates

*By CNN Political Correspondent*

WASHINGTON — In the frantic weeks before a presidential debate, candidates disappear from the campaign trail for what aides cryptically call "debate camp." Behind those closed doors, for over four decades, has often been one man: Robert Barnett, the Washington attorney who has become the Democratic Party's most trusted debate preparation guru.

Barnett's client list reads like a roster of modern Democratic politics — he's helped prepare candidates in presidential and vice presidential debates stretching back to the late 1970s, working with nominees across multiple election cycles. In a wide-ranging conversation, Barnett offered a rare glimpse into the high-pressure, often secretive world of debate prep.

**THE ART OF THE MOCK DEBATE**

"The goal is never to make the candidate a different person," Barnett explained. "It's to make them the best version of themselves under the most artificial, high-pressure circumstances imaginable."

Barnett described his process as building elaborate simulations — full mock debates with stand-ins playing the opposing candidate, complete with podiums, lighting, and even replica stage dimensions when possible. The stand-ins, he noted, study the opponent's mannerisms, speech patterns, and rhetorical tendencies obsessively.

"You need someone who can genuinely get under the candidate's skin the way the real opponent might," he said. "If we're too gentle in practice, we've failed them for the real thing."

**HANDLING THE UNEXPECTED**

Asked about the biggest challenge in debate prep, Barnett didn't hesitate: "You cannot script spontaneity. You can prepare for a thousand scenarios, and the moderator asks the thousand-and-first question."

He emphasized that his job isn't to write answers so much as to build a candidate's comfort with pivoting — taking any question and finding a bridge back to their core message.

"Voters forgive a candidate who doesn't answer the specific question perfectly," Barnett said. "They don't forgive a candidate who looks like they're hiding something or who gets rattled."

**TOWN HALLS: A DIFFERENT ANIMAL**

Barnett was particularly animated discussing town hall formats, which he considers uniquely challenging compared to traditional podium debates.

"A town hall is fundamentally about empathy and connection," he said. "You're not just answering a policy question — you're responding to a human being standing in front of you who often has a personal story attached to that question. Candidates who forget there's a person there, and instead recite talking points, get punished by voters watching at home."

He noted that town halls require different physical training too — teaching candidates to move naturally, make eye contact, and avoid appearing to retreat to a podium or notes, all while managing the same substantive demands as a formal debate.

**THE PSYCHOLOGY OF PREPARATION**

Perhaps most revealing was Barnett's description of debate prep as much psychological as substantive. Candidates, he said, often arrive exhausted, anxious, or overconfident — and part of his job is calibrating their mental state as much as their answers.

"Some candidates need to be built up. Some need a dose of humility. Reading which one you're dealing with on a given day is as important as any briefing book," he said.

He also stressed the importance of managing expectations games played out in the press before debates even happen. "Both campaigns will tell you their candidate is a mediocre debater and the opponent is Cicero reincarnated. It's absurd theater, but it matters because it shapes how performances get judged afterward."

**A LEGACY OF DISCRETION**

Notably, Barnett remained tight-lipped about specifics from his work with individual candidates, citing the confidentiality that he says is essential to the job.

"If candidates think anything said in that prep room might become a story later, they won't be honest with you," he said. "And if they're not honest about their weaknesses with me, we can't fix them before it's too late."

That discretion, combined with his results, is precisely why Barnett's phone keeps ringing every four years — a low-profile fixture in the most high-profile moments of American political life.

# Debate Format Deep Dive: Town Hall vs. Traditional

*A CNN International feature*

**By Michael Holmes**

---

With election season bringing renewed attention to debate formats, I sat down with veteran debate coach Sarah Chen, who has spent over two decades coaching high school and collegiate debate teams and consulting on political debate preparation, to break down how town hall formats differ from traditional podium debates—and what viewers should watch for.

---

**HOLMES: Sarah, thanks for joining us. Let's start basic—what actually defines a town hall debate format versus what we typically see in primary debates?**

CHEN: Sure, so the traditional format is really moderator-driven. You've got candidates behind podiums, a moderator asking questions, structured response times, maybe rebuttals. It's controlled, it's formal, and frankly, it's designed for that.

Town halls flip that. You've got audience members—undecided voters typically—asking the questions directly. Candidates often step out from behind the podium, sometimes walk toward the person asking the question. It's physically and psychologically a different animal.

**HOLMES: Why does that physical element matter so much?**

CHEN: Body language is everything in these settings. When you remove the podium, you remove a barrier—literally and figuratively. Candidates have to think about where their hands go, how they're standing, whether they're making eye contact with the questioner or playing to the cameras. I've seen candidates who are brilliant at the podium completely lose their footing when they have to walk across an open stage.

**HOLMES: We saw that dynamic get a lot of attention in 2016—the Trump-Clinton town hall where he was pacing behind her during her answers.**

CHEN: Exactly, and that's the perfect example. In a traditional format, that moment doesn't exist—you're locked to your podium. In a town hall, suddenly proximity, movement, even how you occupy space becomes part of the message, intentional or not.

**HOLMES: How does the questioning itself change strategy?**

CHEN: Enormously. Moderators in traditional formats tend to ask pointed policy questions, sometimes adversarial follow-ups. Voters in town halls often ask more personal questions—"How has this affected your family?" or "What will you actually do for someone like me?"

Candidates have to shift from debate mode to something closer to conversation mode. The coaching I do differently for town halls focuses heavily on empathy signaling—active listening, repeating back what the voter said, making them feel heard before pivoting to the policy answer.

**HOLMES: Is that harder to fake than podium poise?**

CHEN: Much harder. Audiences—and by extension, television viewers—are very good at detecting when someone's performing empathy versus feeling it. You can prep talking points, but you can't fully prep genuine human connection. That's why town halls can be more revealing, for better or worse.

**HOLMES: Does the format favor a certain type of candidate?**

CHEN: Generally, yes. Candidates with strong retail politics skills—people who've spent time in diners, town squares, that kind of grassroots campaigning—tend to thrive. Career legislators who are used to formal floor debate sometimes struggle with the informality.

That said, I'd caution against oversimplifying it. Some candidates surprise you. Preparation still matters enormously; it's just different preparation.

**HOLMES: How do you prep a candidate differently for town hall than traditional debate?**

CHEN: We do a lot more mock sessions with actual undecided voters, or people playing that role convincingly—not journalists, not staffers. We work on transitions, how to acknowledge a personal story without being dismissive, and how to handle the unpredictability. You genuinely don't know what's coming in a town hall the way you might anticipate moderator questions.

We also spend real time on stagecraft—where to stand, how far to walk, how long to hold eye contact before addressing the broader audience.

**HOLMES: Last question—as a viewer, what should we be watching for?**

CHEN: Watch how candidates handle the moments they didn't script. Watch whether they actually answer the person in front of them or use the question as a springboard to a stump speech. That gap—between genuine responsiveness and rehearsed pivoting—tells you a lot about a candidate, maybe more than the traditional format ever could.

**HOLMES: Sarah Chen, appreciate the insight.**

CHEN: Thanks for having me.

---

*This interview has been edited for length and clarity.*

# The Debate Whisperer: An Interview with Robert Barnett

*A conversation exploring the career of Washington attorney Robert Barnett, who has prepared presidential and vice presidential candidates for televised debates since 1976, a role that has made him one of the most quietly influential figures in modern American politics.*

---

**Q: You've prepared candidates for debates across nearly five decades now. How did you first get pulled into this world?**

**BARNETT:** It really started almost by accident. I was a young lawyer working in Democratic politics, and I got tapped to help with debate preparation during the Carter years. Nobody thought of it as a specialty back then—it was just something that needed doing, and I happened to be available and interested in the mechanics of it. I found I had a knack for anticipating lines of attack, for thinking like an opponent. That's really the whole job in a nutshell: you have to become the person your candidate is going to stand across from.

**Q: You played Geraldine Ferraro's opponent, and later prepped Ferraro herself in 1984. What was that experience like, given the historic nature of her candidacy?**

**BARNETT:** That was a landmark moment, obviously—the first woman on a major party ticket. There was enormous pressure, and a lot of it was unfair pressure, frankly. She was going to be judged by a different standard than any man in that position, and we knew it. My job was to make sure she was over-prepared, so that no matter what curveball came her way, she'd have already seen a version of it in the practice sessions. You try to strip away the historic weight of the moment and just focus on: what are the questions, what are the traps, how do you pivot to your strengths.

**Q: Michael Dukakis in 1988 is remembered for one particularly rough moment—the death penalty question about his wife. Looking back, what did that teach you about debate prep?**

**BARNETT:** That moment is taught in classrooms now, unfortunately for him. What it underscored for me is that you can prepare someone on policy all day long, but you also have to prepare them emotionally—for a gut-punch question designed to catch you flat-footed. The lesson I took from it, and applied ever after, was that you have to run the worst-case-scenario question, the one that makes everyone in the room wince, and you have to run it more than once. You don't let a candidate face that question for the first time on a stage in front of eighty million people.

**Q: You've had a long association with the Clintons—prepping Bill Clinton multiple times and later Hillary Clinton. How does prep differ from candidate to candidate?**

**BARNETT:** Every candidate is genuinely different. Bill Clinton was a phenomenon—an enormous natural gift for connecting with an audience, for finding warmth even in a hostile exchange. My job with him was less about generating answers and more about discipline and pacing, making sure he didn't run over on time because he had so much he wanted to say. Hillary was more of a policy maximalist by instinct, and part of the work was about helping her be crisp, be relatable, translate depth of knowledge into something that felt human and direct rather than like a briefing document.

**Q: You also played Joe Lieberman for Dick Cheney's benefit, and prepared Cheney himself for his vice presidential debates. What's unique about VP debate prep versus the top of the ticket?**

**BARNETT:** The vice presidential debate has its own strange chemistry. You're often facing an opponent who is more of a wild card, so you spend a lot of time trying to model unpredictability. With Cheney, part of the challenge was stylistic—he was not a natural showman, and nobody was going to turn him into one, nor should they have tried. So we focused on substance, gravitas, and command of the material, and let that be the personality. Trying to force a candidate into a mode that isn't authentically theirs is one of the biggest mistakes you can make in this business.

**Q: After all these decades, what do you think people misunderstand about what a debate coach actually does?**

**BARNETT:** People imagine we're feeding candidates clever one-liners, and sure, there's some of that. But the real work is architecture, not decoration. It's understanding the format, understanding the opponent's own vulnerabilities and playbook, building a candidate's message discipline so they can say what they need to say regardless of the question asked, and building resilience so a bad moment doesn't spiral into a bad night. If I've done my job right, nobody in the audience thinks about me at all. They just think they watched their candidate at their best.

**Q: Final question—after Ferraro, Dukakis, the Clintons, Cheney, and so many others, is there a common thread that ties this career together?**

**BARNETT:** Humility, honestly. You realize very quickly that you don't control the outcome—the candidate walks out on that stage alone, and anything can happen. What you can do is make sure they've faced every hard question in the privacy of a rehearsal room first, so that nothing on the real night feels entirely new. That's the whole job, distilled: make the unfamiliar familiar, and then get out of the way.

---

*Robert Barnett's decades of behind-the-scenes debate preparation reflect a broader, largely invisible infrastructure of American electoral politics—one where careful rehearsal, not raw spontaneity, often determines what voters see as authentic performance under pressure.*

# The Man Behind the Podium: A Washington Insider's Decades of Debate Prep

*CNN Exclusive Interview*

For more than three decades, one Washington attorney has operated in the shadows of American presidential politics, helping candidates from both parties prepare for one of the most high-pressure moments in any campaign: the presidential debate. He's worked with nominees you'd recognize immediately, though he's asked that we keep his current client list confidential—a courtesy he says is essential to maintaining trust across the aisle.

We sat down with him to discuss what actually happens behind closed doors when a candidate prepares to face their opponent on a national stage.

**CNN: How did you get into this line of work?**

"Honestly, by accident. I was doing legal work for a campaign back in the early 1980s, and someone said, 'You're good at arguing both sides—why don't you play the opponent in mock debates?' I didn't think much of it at the time. But there's a skill to it that most people don't appreciate. You have to become the other candidate. You have to think like them, anticipate their attacks, even adopt their verbal tics. It's part law, part theater, part psychological warfare."

**CNN: What's the biggest misconception people have about debate prep?**

"That it's about memorizing facts. It's not. Any candidate running for president already knows policy—or has people who can brief them. The real work is about temperament. Can you take a punch? Can you pivot without looking evasive? Can you make a 90-second answer feel authentic instead of rehearsed? That's what we drill. Over and over, sometimes for weeks."

**CNN: You've prepared candidates from both parties. How do you navigate that?**

"I take it very seriously. There's a firewall. I don't carry strategy from one campaign to another—that would be a betrayal of trust, and frankly, this town is small enough that word gets around fast if you're not careful. Candidates need to know that what happens in that prep room stays in that prep room."

**CNN: Any memorable stories from your years doing this?**

He laughed before answering this one.

"Oh, I've got to tell you about Geraldine Ferraro. This was 1984, and we were doing rehearsal for her vice-presidential debate against George H.W. Bush. I was playing Bush, and I decided to really commit to the bit—I borrowed a blue suit, practiced his cadence, even worked on that slight patrician lean he had when he made a point.

"So we're going back and forth, and I'm doing my best Bush impression, really leaning into it, and at one point I said something like, 'Well, Congresswoman, I don't think the American people are going to be persuaded by that,' in his voice. And Ferraro just stopped, looked at me, and said, 'You know, you're starting to scare me a little. Go back to being yourself for a second.'

"The whole room cracked up. But that's actually the goal—if you can rattle them a little in practice, in a safe environment, then the real thing feels almost easier by comparison. She went on to more than hold her own in that actual debate, and I'd like to think our sessions helped, even if I did give her a minor scare along the way."

**CNN: What's the hardest part of the job?**

"Telling a candidate something they don't want to hear. You have to be honest even when it's uncomfortable. If someone has a habit of interrupting, or looking irritated when they're challenged, you have to point that out bluntly, because the cameras will catch it and the American people will notice, even if the candidate doesn't realize they're doing it. Diplomacy only goes so far in that room. Sometimes you just have to say, 'That's not working, and here's why.'"

**CNN: Any advice for future candidates preparing for their first debate?**

"Trust the process. And remember it's not a lecture—it's a conversation, even when it's adversarial. The candidates who do best are the ones who can find moments of genuine connection with the audience, even while making sharp arguments. That's what separates a good debate performance from a great one."

# The Art of Becoming Someone Else: Inside the World of Debate Prep

*By CNN Politics*

Every four years, in hotel conference rooms and campaign compounds far from the cameras, a strange kind of political theater plays out. A candidate stands behind a lectern, facing an opponent who isn't really their opponent at all — but someone paid to become them, down to the mannerisms, the verbal tics, and the attack lines.

We sat down with veteran debate prep specialist Marcus Chen, who has coached candidates in three presidential cycles and countless Senate and gubernatorial races, to talk about what it actually takes to play the role of someone's fiercest political rival.

---

**CNN: Let's start simple. What does a debate prep expert actually do?**

**Chen:** People think it's just mock debates, and that's part of it, but it's really a three-part job. First, I have to *become* the opponent — study their speech patterns, their go-to deflections, even how they breathe when they're cornered. Second, I have to anticipate the moderators' questions and the moments that could go sideways. And third, and this is the part people underestimate, I have to help the candidate manage themselves — their adrenaline, their ego, their instinct to over-explain.

**CNN: Walk us through how you "become" a candidate. That sounds almost like acting.**

**Chen:** It is acting, honestly. I'll spend weeks with transcripts — every debate, every town hall, every unscripted press gaggle I can find. I'm listening for rhythm. Does this person speak in short punchy sentences or do they meander? Do they repeat a phrase when they're uncomfortable? Politicians are creatures of habit under pressure. One candidate I studied always said "look" before pivoting away from a hard question. Once you catch that tic, you can predict when they're about to dodge — and more importantly, you can train your client to spot it happening in real time.

I also study body language obsessively. How they stand when they feel confident versus defensive. Whether they point, whether they smile when they're being aggressive — some people smile *more* when they're delivering an attack, which is disarming and effective. If I can replicate that in the room, my candidate isn't blindsided by it on the actual stage.

**CNN: Do you take on their policy positions too, or just the style?**

**Chen:** Both, but the policy is actually the easier part — you can hand someone a briefing book. The harder part is playing their *rhetorical instincts*. What's their attack style? Are they a bulldozer who interrupts, or someone who uses silence and a raised eyebrow to needle the other person? I had one client whose opponent was a master of the backhanded compliment — "I respect my opponent, but clearly they don't understand how this works." That's a specific weapon. You have to drill against that exact tone, not just the general idea of "expect insults."

**CNN: What's the biggest mistake candidates make in prep?**

**Chen:** Over-preparing for facts and under-preparing for feelings. Debates are not decided by who has the better spreadsheet. They're decided by who looks steadier, who seems more human, who doesn't flinch. I've watched incredibly smart candidates lose their composure because they were so focused on being *correct* that they forgot to be *likable* or *calm*.

So a lot of my job is stress-testing emotional control. I'll interrupt them mid-sentence, the way a real opponent might. I'll bring up a family member, a past scandal, something personal — not because it's fair, but because it *might happen*, and the first time your candidate hears that line of attack should never be on the actual stage.

**CNN: Do you use any specific techniques to simulate the pressure of a real debate?**

**Chen:** Absolutely. We do full mock debates with a live studio setup — lighting, lecterns, a timer, sometimes even a mock audience that reacts. I'll bring in a moderator who's been briefed to ask the exact hardball questions we think are coming, plus a few we know will catch them off guard.

I also do what I call "gotcha drills" — rapid-fire, no time to think, where I hit them with the worst possible framing of their record, over and over, until the flinch goes away. The goal isn't to make them numb. It's to make the tenth time they hear an attack feel as manageable as the first time felt overwhelming.

And then there's video review, which is brutal but essential. Watching yourself lose your composure on a giant screen is humbling in a way that notes on paper never are.

**CNN: Is there a moment you're especially proud of — a technique that clearly worked?**

**Chen:** I can't get into specifics, client confidentiality and all that. But I'll say this: the best moments in prep are never the polished answers. They're the moments a candidate gets rattled, says something clumsy, and then we stop, rewind, and figure out *why* it rattled them. That's where the real work happens. By the time they're on stage, the goal is that nothing said to them is actually new. It's just an echo of something they've already survived in a windowless room with me.

**CNN: Last question — after playing so many political figures, does it ever get in your head? Do you start thinking like them?**

**Chen:** *(laughs)* More than I'd like to admit. There's a strange intimacy to studying someone that closely, even someone whose politics you disagree with. You start to understand their fears, not just their talking points. Honestly, that's the job. You can't beat someone in a debate, real or practiced, until you understand what they're actually afraid of losing.

---

*This interview has been edited for length and clarity.*
